verdict: Avoid new castings and forgings exposure in Howrah; lend only to export-order-backed forgers with nil-gearing balance sheets, and then only against monthly covenant packs.
title: Howrah castings & forgings: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
A Howrah foundry melts scrap and pig iron in an induction furnace, pours into moulds, and sells machined or raw castings to auto, railway, and capital-goods buyers; a forger buys billets and hammers or presses them into flanges, axles, and gears. **Cash is made on conversion spread, not on price** — the customer sets the price off a raw-material index, so the foundry earns a fixed per-kg margin and the metal cost passes through. That means the real credit question is never the order book; it is whether the unit keeps its melting hours full and its yield per tonne high. **So when a proposal lands, check furnace utilisation and yield per tonne before you look at turnover; if yield is not disclosed, ask for the last twelve months of melting and despatch registers.**

## Where value and cash sit
Value sits in the finishing shop and in the customer approval — a casting approved for a railway or CV buyer is a sticky annuity, an unapproved one is scrap. Cash sits in receivables, because these buyers pay in 60–90 days while the foundry pays for scrap and power in advance or on delivery. **Capex is heavy and lumpy — furnace, moulding line, machining centre — and it is funded by term debt that outlives the order.** Power is the second-largest cost after metal, so a cluster with weak infrastructure carries a permanent cost handicap. Collect from customer the power tariff per unit and the share of power in total cost; if power is above a fifth of cost, ask how the unit recovers it in price. ## What has broken now
Local reporting is blunt: Howrah's foundry belt, once the 'Sheffield of the East', has faced ageing infrastructure, labour unrest, and a slowdown in investment and technology upgrades, with several foundries relocating to Jharkhand [1][2]. Raw-material price increases and government policy are squeezing the cluster [3]. **The state numbers confirm the local drag — West Bengal GST collections are -1.3% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, and electricity demand is +5.7% against India +9.5% [D].** Nationally, IIP for NIC 24 is only +2.4% YoY [D], and Brent at $113/bbl sits above the $75–100 band [D], which raises freight and power-linked costs. Note the local sources are from March–July 2026 and are qualitative, not financial. ## Where the growth is — and who to avoid
Peer results split cleanly. Ramkrishna Forgings grew revenue 54.9% YoY to Rs 1,405 crore with EBITDA margin at 18.23% and Rs 673 crore of new orders [6]; Happy Forgings carries a ~Rs 950 crore order book, ~60% export [5], and grew quarterly revenue 20.4% [7]. Nelcast, more CV-domestic, saw revenue fall to Rs 335 crore in Q2FY25 from Rs 362.6 crore [4]. **Pursue the export-order forger and the approved-supplier machining unit; avoid the job-work foundry selling to local traders on 90-day credit.** Ramkrishna is only 'considering' a Howrah unit, subject to land and incentives [1] — treat that as news, not a pipeline. ## How to grow safely
Structure against the order, not the balance sheet: receivables-backed limits, escrow of buyer payments, and a term loan sized to the approved customer's offtake. **Take a monthly stock-and-receivable statement, power bills, and a melting-hours log — power consumption is the hardest number to fake.** Rating evidence supports this discipline: one forger runs near-nil gearing with TOL/TNW at 0.3 times [8], while a casting peer sits at CRISIL BB/A4+ [9] and another at 8.4% OPM with interest cover of 3.8 times [11]. If gearing exceeds 2 times or interest cover falls below 2, decline.
